source.title: Scalable Multi-Domain Adaptation of Language Models using Modular Experts
source.authors: Peter Schafhalter; Shun Liao; Yan-Qi Zhou; C. Yeh; A. Kandoor; J. Laudon

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream test accuracy while varying adaptation parameters and training examples, but it does not reproduce pretraining-loss scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 and its accompanying text report next-token accuracy for domain adaptation as added expert/adapter parameters and training examples vary. These results bear on V6's downstream-performance aspect, but not on held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fitted power laws, or compute-optimal allocation. Values are shown in plots without reported point estimates. The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as background for its evaluation metric; cited scaling-law results are not extracted.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper: it compares its MoDE adapter with LoRA and full fine-tuning on one 1.58B backbone. The Section 4.3 'scalability' results measure next-token accuracy on a held-out Code set as adapter parameters or fine-tuning examples grow. They show the proposed method's performance against baselines. None of them concern pretraining loss, base-model scale, compute-optimal allocation, or a fitted power law. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only to justify next-token accuracy as the evaluation metric. V6 does not apply: it concerns downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss, not adapter size within one fixed model. V5 does not apply either: no power-law form is fitted or claimed for fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that MoDE scales better than LoRA with added parameters and training data. They also conclude it matches full fine-tuning on target domains with about 1.5–1.65% better English retention, beats LoRA by 1.4% on average, and enables MPMD sharding that trains up to 38% faster.
record.recipe_differences: This is a domain-adaptation method comparison, not a reproduction of the original pretraining-loss scaling-law methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream accuracy trend differs between MoDE and LoRA; LoRA performs better on smaller datasets up to approximately 1k examples and plateaus beyond that.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out next-token accuracy during adaptation rises with the number of added expert transformer layers: Table 3 Code accuracy goes from 76.98 to 77.96. With LoRA, accuracy stays flat as rank grows and collapses at rank 2048 (Table 2: 66.55). Accuracy also grows with fine-tuning examples for MoDE but plateaus above about 1k for LoRA (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptation accuracy grows with adapter capacity and fine-tuning data when full transformer-layer experts are added, but not with low-rank adapters.

record.problems: The scale trends are presented in plots without point estimates or uncertainty; the experiments use one 1.58 billion-parameter PLM backbone and do not fit or test a power law.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count. The block and expert-layer ablations change parameter count, so they do not test this.
No power-law form is fitted for fine-tuning or adaptation.
Downstream performance as a function of base-model scale or pretraining loss.
Fit or setup dependence of exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tests' and 'supports' labels are dropped. Adapter-size and fine-tuning-data trends on one fixed 1.58B backbone are a comparison of the authors' method with baselines. They do not bear on downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss. No power law is fitted, and no scaling-law version is assessed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effect of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds in adaptation or other training regimes.
The study tests task accuracy against adaptation parameters and training examples, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or base-model scale.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: MoDE
rows.operation_detail: Increased expert transformer layers and additional parameters for Code adaptation.
rows.value: figure only; text says accuracy improves continuously as more parameters are added
rows.note: The plotted trend concerns added adaptation parameters, not scaling the pretrained model itself.
rows.check: Measures the authors' own method's held-out Code next-token accuracy against added adapter parameters on a fixed backbone. This is a method comparison, not base-model scale or pretraining loss, so it bears on no version. Figure-only trend, with no power-law fit.

rows.subject: LoRA
rows.operation_detail: Increased LoRA rank and additional parameters for Code adaptation.
rows.value: figure only; text says LoRA struggles to turn additional parameters into higher accuracy
rows.note: The textual description characterizes gains from added adaptation parameters as limited.
rows.check: LoRA baseline in the authors' method comparison, not a scaling-law measurement. Table 2 gives numbers: Code accuracy is flat around 76.0–76.5 from rank 8 to 1024, then drops to 66.55 at rank 2048. That is flat then falling, not merely partial; the row should cite Table 2.

rows.subject: MoDE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Code datasets with varying numbers of examples, keeping training steps the same.
rows.value: figure only; text says accuracy continues to improve as the number of training examples increases
rows.note: This is adaptation-data scaling, not a fit of pretraining loss against token count.
rows.check: Fine-tuning data scaling for the authors' own method on a single fixed backbone, in a method comparison. Not pretraining tokens and not downstream versus scale. Figure-only trend.

rows.subject: LoRA
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Code datasets with varying numbers of examples, keeping training steps the same.
rows.value: figure only; text says LoRA performs better on smaller datasets up to approximately 1k examples, then its accuracy plateaus above one thousand examples
rows.note: LoRA does better at small data sizes but does not keep improving as the dataset grows.
rows.check: LoRA comparator in a method comparison. Accuracy plateaus beyond about 1k fine-tuning examples. Bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
